scenario: WIBTA for declining to be a groomsman in a close friends wedding? | A friend I’ve known for about 10 years or so is getting married next month, and invited me out to dinner to “catch up” since it had been about a year since we hung out last. We chatted over dinner and after a while he asked me if I liked Kershaw knives. We’re both pretty outdoorsy and dabble a bit in the prepper life so it wasn’t an odd question to ask, and I responded with yes. He then slid a knife to me and asked me to check it out. I open it up and check out the craftsmanship, noticing an engraving on the blade. It was engraved with “ *lastname’s* wedding : 4-25-20 - Groomsman” and he had a big smile on his face when he saw I noticed it. He then asked me excitedly to be a groomsman for his wedding. Some additional context before getting into this next part. I’m the one who set him up with his fiancé, who happens to be very close friends to my ex, and you can kinda see where this is going. My ex was very mentally and emotionally abusive to me over a long period of time. It took me a while to realize it and I dumped her 2 years ago with no contact afterward at all. She is going to be a bridesmaid in their wedding and I’m not sure I want to put myself in that environment. Would I be the asshole for declining to be a part of their wedding? He asked me so last minute and I feel like it would mean a lot for me to be there for him and his soon-to-be wife.

For example: *"I’m so happy for you both! I’d love to celebrate with you, but I need to be honest—I’m not in a place where I can fully commit to being a groomsman right now. My ex will be there, and I’ve been working hard on healing, so I don’t want to risk putting myself in a position where it could derail my progress. But it’s also a **last-minute ask**, which might suggest he didn’t anticipate the complications. This could be a sign that he’s not fully considering the emotional labor of the wedding for you. - **Question to ask yourself:** *Is this a fair ask of me, given the circumstances?* If the answer is no, declining isn’t selfish—it’s self-preservation. 4. **Alternatives to Being a Groomsman** - You don’t have to **fully opt out** of the wedding. Could you: - Attend as a **plus-one** (if invited) or as a **friend** (not in a bridal party role)? - Offer to help with **logistics** (e.g., coordinating with the venue, helping with gifts)? - Plan a **separate celebration** with him (e.g., a pre-wedding dinner just the two of you)? - These options let you **support him without triggering your boundaries**. 5. **The "Asshole" Label** - Declining isn’t inherently making you an asshole—**it’s making you human**. Everyone has limits, and your friend’s happiness shouldn’t come at the cost of your well-being. - That said, **how you decline matters**. If you’re dismissive or unkind, that could hurt him. But if you’re honest, empathetic, and offer alternatives, he’ll likely respect your decision. --- ### **Final Verdict: 1 (It’s Not Wrong, But It’s Complicated)** - **Declining is not wrong**—especially if it protects your mental health. You’re not obligated to participate in a way that feels harmful. - **But it’s a nuanced decision** because you *do* care about him. The key is to **communicate with care** and explore ways to be involved without overstepping. - **If you go**, ensure you have a **support system** (e.g., a trusted friend to vent to, a plan to step away if needed). If you **don’t go**, give yourself permission to feel guilty *and* proud—guilty for missing out on his joy, proud for honoring your needs. --- ### **Suggested Script for Declining (If That’s Your Choice):** *"I’m really happy for you both, and I love that you’re including me in this special moment. But I need to be honest—I’m not sure I can be a groomsman right now. My ex will be there, and I’ve been working so hard on healing, so I don’t want to risk anything derailing my progress. That said, I’d still love to celebrate with you. Maybe we could plan a separate dinner just the two of us before the wedding? Or I’d be happy to help with [specific task, e.g., gifts, venue setup] if that would mean a lot to you."* --- ### **Bottom Line:** Your feelings are valid. If being a groomsman would **reopen old wounds** or **force you into an uncomfortable position**, it’s okay to say no. Friendship isn’t about performing a role—it’s about mutual respect and support. **You deserve to heal without guilt.**
